title: Liber De Promissionibus Et Praedictionibus Dei A Nonnullis [Incertus]
author: Prosperus Aquitanus
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0237.stoa011.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: pectus et brachia ejus argentea, Macedonicum Septentrionis ; venter et femora aerea, Punicum Meridiani ; crura ferrea et digiti pedum partim ferrei, partim fictiles, ultimum Romanum, videlicet Occidentis, sicut et vir eruditissimus Orosius historiographus posuit. Quod regnum tamquam ferrum comminuit omnia, et domnii. Christi quoque regnum subjungit Daniel in lapide abscisso de monte sine manibus concidentinm (Ibid., 44 et 45). tamquam sine manibus complectentium Deum hominem ex Virgine natum.
passages.english: its chest and arms of silver, the Macedonian [kingdom] of the North; its belly and thighs of bronze, the Punic [kingdom] of the South; its legs of iron and the toes of its feet partly of iron, partly of clay, the last, the Roman, that is, of the West, just as the most learned man Orosius the historian also set it down. This kingdom, like iron, crushes all things and subdues [them]. Daniel also adds the kingdom of Christ, in the stone cut from the mountain without hands, falling (ibid., 44 and 45), as if without the hands of those embracing [it], God [made] man, born of the Virgin.
passages.notes: 'et domnii' is corrupt; rendered 'and subdues [them]' (perhaps for 'et domat'). 'concidentinm' read as 'concidentem'. The final clause ('tamquam sine manibus complectentium') is obscure, possibly 'without the hands of men coupling', i.e. without human intercourse.

passages.original: XXVIII, 2, etc.): cujus portam orientalem clausam semper ostendit, dicens : Hæc porta clausa crit, solus princeps sacerdotum n transibit per eam, et ipsa clausa erit principi (Ezech. XLIV, 2); Mariæ virginalem nterum signans. quæ semper urgo integra protulit Salvatorem. Solus enim Christus Dominus, ut ait beatæ memoriæ Augustinus episcopus, a per inviolata matris virginea viscera, membra infantis eduxit, qui post resurrectionem per clausa ostia membra juvenis introduxit : solus pecratum. non habens infrantilis ætatis exortu, qui peccatum non habuit grandioris .latis accessu. ipso dicente : Ecce venit princeps hujus mundi, et in me nihil inveniet (Joan. XIV, 30).
passages.english: XXVIII, 2, etc.): he shows its eastern gate always shut, saying: "This gate shall be shut; the prince of priests alone shall pass through it, and it shall be shut for the prince" (Ezek. 44:2), signifying the virginal womb of Mary, who, always a virgin, brought forth the Saviour intact. For Christ the Lord alone, as Augustine the bishop of blessed memory says, brought out the limbs of an infant through the inviolate virginal womb of his mother, who after the resurrection brought in the limbs of a young man through closed doors: he alone had no sin at the birth of infancy, who had no sin on reaching a greater age, as he himself says: "Behold, the prince of this world comes, and he will find nothing in me" (John 14:30).
passages.notes: 'grandioris .latis' read as 'grandioris aetatis'. The final clause of the gate quotation ('clausa erit principi') is translated as it stands.

passages.original: 92 Sine apud Machabæos nliimus dux ei pontifex fuit Hircanus ( I Mach. xvi, 24). Nam fratrem ejus Aristobolum Pompeius magistratus populi Romani, dum Jerosolymam expugnaret, vinctum cum liberis Romam misit, sicut Josephi narrat Historia. a Impleta tamen Jacob patriarchæ prophetia dicentis : Non deficiet princeps ex Juda, neque dux de femoribus ejus, donec veniat cui rrposita sunt omnia, et ipse erit exspectatio gentium (Gen.
passages.english: But among the Maccabees the last leader and high priest was Hyrcanus (1 Macc. 16:24). For his brother Aristobulus was sent bound with his children to Rome by Pompey, magistrate of the Roman people, when he was storming Jerusalem, as the History of Josephus relates. Yet the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob was fulfilled, who said: "A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom all things are laid up, and he shall be the expectation of the nations" (Gen.
passages.notes: 'Sine' read as 'Sed'; 'nliimus' as 'ultimus'; 'rrposita' as 'reposita'. The passage breaks off mid-reference.

passages.original: 3. David propheta : A summo coelo , ait, egressio ejus. Et iterum : Regnum tuum, regnum omnium sæculorum (Psal. XVIII, 7; et CXLIV, 13). Item ipse : Regnavit Dominus super omnes gentes (P*. XLVI, 9). Ei Isaias : Reqem cum claritate videbitis. Item : Ecce Rex tuus, ahi, venit sedens super nubem lenem (Isa. XXXIII, i?; et XIX, 1), carnem scilicet nullum pondus habenleui peccati. Firmat hæc Evangelium Matthæi, dicens : Magi ab Oriente venerunt dicentes : Ubi est qui natus est Rex Judæorum (Matt. II, 1)? Testatur et Paulus : Regi, ait, sæculorum. Et iterum : Ostendet beatus ei solus potens Rex regum, et Dominus dominorum (I filii. I, 17; vi, 15). Fateturque Sibylla: E cælo rex adveniet per sæcla futurus.
passages.english: 3. David the prophet says: "His going forth is from the highest heaven." And again: "Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages" (Ps. 18:7; 144:13). Also the same: "The Lord has reigned over all nations" (Ps. 46:9). And Isaiah: "You will see the King in glory." Also: "Behold, your King," he says, "comes sitting upon a light cloud" (Isa. 33:17; 19:1), that is, flesh having no weight of sin. The Gospel of Matthew confirms these things, saying: "Magi came from the East, saying: Where is he who is born King of the Jews?" (Matt. 2:1). Paul too bears witness: "To the King of the ages," he says. And again: "The blessed and only Mighty One, the King of kings and Lord of lords, will show" (1 Tim. 1:17; 6:15). And the Sibyl declares: "From heaven will come the king who shall be for the ages."

passages.original: I. David propheta : Misit, at, Verbum suum, et , sanavit eos (Ps. evi, 20). Et Jeremias: Bic Deus noster, et non est alius absque eo qui invenit omnem viam prudentiæ, et ddit eam Ja ob b electo sibi : post hæc in terris visus est et cum hominibus conversatus est (Baruch III, 36, etc.). Et Habacuc propheta : Ambulavit, ait, Verbum, et exiit in campos (Habac. II, 3, sec. LXX). c Firmai hæc Joannes evangelista, dicens : Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (Joan. I, 14). Testatur et Paulus : Cum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est d esse æqualis Deo; sed semetipsum exinanivit formam servi accipient, in similitudinem hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut home. Fateturque Sibylla : Scilicet e in carne præsens ut judicet orbem.
passages.english: 4. David the prophet: "He sent," he says, "his Word, and healed them" (Ps. 106:20). And Jeremiah: "This is our God, and there is no other besides him, who found out every way of understanding and gave it to Jacob, his chosen one; after this he was seen on earth and lived among men" (Baruch 3:36, etc.). And Habakkuk the prophet: "The Word walked," he says, "and went out into the fields" (Hab. 3:5, according to the Septuagint). John the evangelist confirms these things, saying: "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). Paul too bears witness: "Though he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man." And the Sibyl declares: "Namely, present in the flesh to judge the world."
passages.notes: The unit number 'I.' is likely a misread '4.'. The passage is attributed to Jeremiah though cited from Baruch.

passages.original: 5. Isaias propheta : Ecce. ait. Virgo in utero accipiet et pariet filium, et vocabitis nomen ejus Emmanuel (Isa. VII, 14); quod g interpretatur, Nobiscum Deus. Firmat hoc Lucas evangelista, dicens : Missus est Gabriel angelus ad Virginem desponsatam, cui nomen erat Maria: qui et ingressus sic eam salutavit: Ave, inquit v gratia plena, Dominus tecum. Et paulo post : Spiritus sanctus, ait, superveniet in te, et virtus Altiosimi obumbrabit tibi: propterea quod nascetur ex te sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei (Ibid. 35). Testatur et Paulus dicens : Cum autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum factum ex muliere (Gal. IV, 4); Hebræum locutionem sequens, quæ omnes feminas mulieres nominat. Fatelur et Sibylla: Deum cernent (inquit) incredulus, alque fidelis. Dicit Maro : Jam nova progenies cœlo demittitur alto Jam redit et virgo. Redit, dixit, quia virgo adhuc Eva mortem intulit mundo, rediens virgo Maria h protulit Salvatorem.
passages.english: 5. Isaiah the prophet: "Behold," he says, "a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel" (Isa. 7:14), which is interpreted, God with us. Luke the evangelist confirms this, saying: "The angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin betrothed, whose name was Mary; and coming in he greeted her thus: Hail, he said, full of grace, the Lord is with you." And a little later: "The Holy Spirit," he says, "will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God" (ibid. 35). Paul too bears witness, saying: "But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman" (Gal. 4:4), following the Hebrew idiom, which calls all females women. The Sibyl too declares: "The unbeliever and the faithful," she says, "will see God." Maro says: "Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven; now the virgin too returns." He said "returns" because, as Eve while still a virgin brought death into the world, the virgin Mary, returning, brought forth the Saviour.

passages.original: 6. Isaias propheta : Agnovit, ait, bos possessorem suum, et asinus præsepe domini sui (Isa. I, 3). Et Habacuc : In medio, inquit, J duum animalium cognosceris (Habac. III, 2, sec. LXX). Firmat hæc Lucas evangelista, dicens : Cum autem impleti sunt dies Mariæ, peperit filium, et pannis eum involvit, et posuit in præsepe, quoniam non erat locus in diversorio (Luc. II, 6, 7), Et Angelus ad pastores : Natus est x vobis, ait, Christus Dominus in civitate David; et hoc vobis signum : Invenietis infantem pannis obvolutum et positum in præcepe (Ibid., 11). Testatur et Paulus, dicens : Pauper factus est, cum dives ene, ut ejus paupertate not ditaremur (I Cor. VIII, 9). Fa- tetur ei Sibylla : Cum jacet incultus densis 1 in vepribus orbis.
passages.english: 6. Isaiah the prophet: "The ox," he says, "has known its owner, and the ass its master's manger" (Isa. 1:3). And Habakkuk: "In the midst of two animals," he says, "you will be known" (Hab. 3:2, according to the Septuagint). Luke the evangelist confirms these things, saying: "When Mary's days were fulfilled, she bore a son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room in the inn" (Luke 2:6–7). And the angel to the shepherds: "Christ the Lord," he says, "is born to you in the city of David; and this is a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger" (ibid., 11). Paul too bears witness, saying: "He became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be made rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). And the Sibyl declares: "When the world lies untilled among dense thorn-bushes."

passages.original: balaam propheta ex gentibus, Orietur, inquit, stella ex Jacob, et exsurget homo a Israel, et confringet omnia regna terræ (Num. XXIV, 17). Et Isaia3 propheta : Gentium populus, ait, sedens in tenebris vidit n lucem magnam (Isa. VII, 2). Et David dixit : Reges Tharsis et insulæ munera offerent, reges Arabum et Saba dona adducent (Ps. LXXI, 10). Item Isaias : Omnes a Saba venient, ferentes aurum, thus et lapidem pretiosam, salutare Domini bene nuntiabunt (Isa. LX , 6). Firmat haec Matthæus evangelisia, dicens : Ecce stella quam viderant Magi in Oriente, præibat eos, donec venit et stelit supra locum ubi erat puer. Videntes autem stellam, gavisi sunt gaudio magno. Ingressi itaque invenerunt puerum et matrem ejus. Apertisque thesauris obtulerunt ei munera : aurum, ut Regi; thus. at Sacerdoti; et myrrham, o ut morituro pro nobis (Matth. II, 9, etc.). Testatur et Paulus : Deus, inquit, qui dixit de tenebris lumen clarescere, claruit in rordibus nostris : ad illuminationem gloriæ scientiæ ejus P in faciem Christi Jesu (II Cor. IT, 6); fateturque Sibylla, dicens : Exuret terras ignis, q pontumque polumque. Dicit et Maro quedam congrua (Æneid. ii, v. 694, 700): Stella facem ducens multa cum luce cucurrit: r Muneribus cumulant, et sanctum sidus adorant.
passages.english: Balaam, a prophet from the gentiles: "A star shall rise," he says, "out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and shall break all the kingdoms of the earth" (Num. 24:17). And Isaiah the prophet: "The people of the nations," he says, "sitting in darkness, has seen a great light" (Isa. 9:2). And David said: "The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba will bring presents" (Ps. 71:10). Also Isaiah: "All will come from Sheba, bringing gold, incense and precious stone; they will proclaim well the salvation of the Lord" (Isa. 60:6). Matthew the evangelist confirms these things, saying: "Behold, the star which the Magi had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was. Seeing the star, they rejoiced with great joy. Going in, they found the child and his mother. And opening their treasures they offered him gifts: gold, as to a King; incense, as to a Priest; and myrrh, as to one who would die for us" (Matt. 2:9, etc.). Paul too bears witness: "God," he says, "who said light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ Jesus" (2 Cor. 4:6). And the Sibyl declares, saying: "Fire will burn up the lands, the sea and the sky." And Maro says some fitting things (Aeneid 2.694, 700): "A star drawing a torch ran with much light"; "they heap [them] with gifts, and adore the holy star."
passages.notes: The reference 'Isa. VII, 2' should be Isa. 9:2. The second Virgil line is not from Aeneid 2 as given.

passages.original: 1 Venantibus dedit monte: altissimos cervis ; petram refugium erinaciis (Ps. CIII, 18), et leporibus;, piscantibus vero, Volucres cœli et pisces maria , qui perambulant sentitas maris (Ps.VIII, 9). Quod breviter exponit David, dicens : Principes populorum convenerunt cum Deo Abraham (Ps. XLVI, 10). Fatetur et Sibylla: Celsum cum sanctis; aevi jam termino in ipso.
passages.english: To the hunters he gave the high mountains for the stags, the rock a refuge for the hedgehogs (Ps. 103:18) and the hares; but to the fishers, "the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea" (Ps. 8:9). David explains this briefly, saying: "The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham" (Ps. 46:10). The Sibyl too declares: "On high with the saints, at the very end of the age."
passages.notes: 'sentitas' read as 'semitas'. The Sibyl line is fragmentary and its sense is uncertain.

passages.original: zantur, et beatus qui non fuerit scandalizatus in me (Matth. XI, it etc ). Testatur et Petrus in Actibus Apos olorum : Jesus, ait, qui venit benefaciens et curans in plebe omnem infirmitatem, quia Deus erat in eo (Act. x, 38). Dicit ad hæc et Maro (Eadem Eclog. IV, v. 15); Ipse deum vitam accipiet.
passages.english: [...the poor have the gospel preach]ed to them, and blessed is he who is not scandalized in me (Matt. 11[:5–6], etc.). Peter too bears witness in the Acts of the Apostles: "Jesus," he says, "who came doing good and healing every infirmity among the people, because God was in him" (Acts 10:38). To this Maro also says (same Eclogue 4, line 15): "He shall receive the life of a god."
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-word: "zantur" completes "evangelizantur" from the preceding context ("pauperes evangeli-zantur", "the poor have the gospel preached to them"). The opening words are supplied in brackets from that context. The Gospel quotation is in fact Matthew 11 (also Luke 7), although the context before ascribes it to Mark. The reference "it etc" is garbled in the scan; it presumably stands for verses 5–6. "Apos olorum" is read as "Apostolorum". Maro is Virgil. "Ipse deum vitam accipiet" is the Fourth Eclogue, line 15, "ille deum vitam accipiet"; "deum" is the old genitive plural, so the line literally means "he shall receive the life of the gods." It is rendered here in the singular, in keeping with the author's Christian reading.

passages.original: 15. David propheta : In mari est ria tua, et semilæ tuæ in aquis multis (Ps. IXXVI, 20). Dicit et Habacuc : Dispergens aquas d itineris, dedit abyssus vocem suam (Habac. III, 10). FirmianI hæc Evangelium Matthæi, dicens : Quarta autem noctis vigilia venit Jesus ad discipulos suos, ambulans supra mare. Videte. vero eum discipuli timuerunt, dicentes: Quia phantasma est. Accedens autem ad eos Jesus, dxit eis: Ego sum, nolite timere (Matth. XIV, 25, etc.). Salomon etiam dicit : Dedisti in mari viam et inter fluctus semitam firmissimam , ostendens quoniam potes etiam sine rate transeuntes mare servare (Sap. XIV, 3). Quod etiam in Petro Jesus fecisse cognoscitur (Matth. XIV, 3). Testatur et Paulus in naufragio adstuisse sibi Jesum, dicentem : Ne timeas, Paule; ecce enim donavit tibi Deus omnes qui tecum navigant (Act. XXVII, 24). Ex quibus nullus hominum periit nisi navis tantum. Siby la vero e supra dicta ad utrumque respondit: Exuret terras ignis, pontumque i polumque.
passages.english: 15. The prophet David [says]: "Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters" (Ps. 76:20). And Habakkuk says: "Scattering the waters of the way, the deep gave forth its voice" (Hab. 3:10). The Gospel of Matthew confirms these things, saying: "In the fourth watch of the night Jesus came to his disciples, walking on the sea. But when the disciples saw him they were afraid, saying: It is a ghost. But Jesus, coming to them, said to them: It is I, do not be afraid" (Matt. 14:25 etc.). Solomon also says: "You have given a way in the sea and a most firm path among the waves, showing that you can save even those who cross the sea without a boat" (Wis. 14:3). Jesus is known to have done this also in the case of Peter (Matt. 14). Paul too testifies that in the shipwreck Jesus stood by him, saying: "Do not be afraid, Paul; for see, God has granted you all who sail with you" (Acts 27:24). Of these no one perished, only the ship. And the Sibyl mentioned above answered to both: "Fire will burn up the lands, and the sea and the sky."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (ria = via, semitæ, Videntes, dixit, Sibylla, etc.). "Firmiant" read as "Firmat". The Matthew reference for Peter should be 14:29. "Ad utrumque" (to both) is unclear; it may mean to both kinds of testimony, or to both sea and land.

passages.original: Et abiit, et exiit foras, ut eum traderet Judaeis. Et iterum abiit Judas, et retulit argentum principibus sacerdotum, dicens Peccavi tradendo sanguinem justum (Marc. XIV, 18 ; Luc. XIII, 21; Matth. XXVII, 4). Testatur et Paulus : Dominus Jesus, ait, ea nocte qua tradebatur, accepit panem (I Cor. XI, 23); et caetera qum usque ad traditionem acta sunt. Fateturque Sibylla : Tradetur, sonles a eternum flamma cremabit.
passages.english: And he went away and went outside, to betray him to the Jews. And again Judas went away and brought back the silver to the chief priests, saying: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood" (Mark 14:18; Luke 22:21; Matt. 27:4). Paul too testifies: "The Lord Jesus," he says, "on the night on which he was betrayed, took bread" (1 Cor. 11:23), and the other things that were done up to the betrayal. And the Sibyl declares: "He will be betrayed; the eternal flame will burn the guilty."
passages.notes: "sonles a eternum" read as "sontes aeterna" (the guilty ... eternal), which gives the line its sense.

passages.original: 20. Per Isaiam prophetam : Ipse dorsum meum, ait, posui ad flagella, maxillus vero meas ad palmas, faciem vero meam non averti a fœditate sputorum (Isa. L. 6). Et Jeremias dicit: Dabit percutienti se maxillam, c saturabitur opprobriis (Thren. m, 30). Et hæc omnes evangelistæ confirmant, quod flagellatum Jesum eis Pilatus traddit crucifugendum, cique pilmas et colaphos dabant, dicentes : Prophetiza nobis, Christe, quis te percussit (Matth. XXVI, 67)? Testatur in his et Petrus apostolus, dicens : Christus pro d nobis passus eat, vob is relinquens exemplum ut sequammi vestigia eius. Qui eum molediceretur, non remaledice- bat; cum pateretur, non comminabatur; commendabat autem e judicanti se juste (I Petr. II, 21 seq.). Fatetur Sibylla alia : c f In manus, inquit, impiorum postea veniet, dabunt Deo alapas manibus incestis. ct impurato ore exspuent venenatos sputos. Dabit vero ipse ad verbera sanctum dorsum, et colaphos accipiens tacebat; ne quis agnoscat quod Verbum, vel unde veniat.» Quæ omnia inpleta in Christo Uomiuo, omnis jam mundus agnoscit.
passages.english: 20. Through the prophet Isaiah: "I myself," he says, "have set my back to the scourges and my cheeks to the slaps, and I did not turn my face away from the filth of spitting" (Isa. 50:6). And Jeremiah says: "He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he will be filled with reproaches" (Lam. 3:30). And all the evangelists confirm these things: that Pilate handed Jesus over to them, scourged, to be crucified, and that they gave him slaps and blows, saying: "Prophesy to us, Christ, who struck you?" (Matt. 26:67). The apostle Peter too testifies to these things, saying: "Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you may follow in his footsteps. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten; but he committed [himself] to the one who judges justly" (1 Pet. 2:21 ff.). Another Sibyl declares: "Afterwards," she says, "he will come into the hands of the wicked; they will give God slaps with unchaste hands, and with impure mouth they will spit poisoned spittle. But he will give his holy back to the lashes, and receiving blows he kept silent, so that no one might recognise that [he is] the Word, or where he comes from." The whole world now recognises that all these things were fulfilled in Christ the Lord.
passages.notes: Many scanning errors corrected (maxillas, tradidit crucifigendum, palmas, est, sequamini, malediceretur, Domino). The shift from future to past tense ("kept silent") is in the text.

passages.original: 21. Per David h ipse : Conversus sum, ait, in ærumna, dum infigeretur spina (Ps. XXXI, 4). Et hoc evangelistæ confirmant, quod spineam coronam i imposuerunt capiti ejus, et crucem suam portans M'it (Matth. xxvii, 29; Marc. xv, 17; Joan. xix, 18). Hoc etiam aries ille signavit, qui III spinis cornibus detentus immolatus est pro Isaac (Gen. XXII, 13). Fatetur et Sibylla : « Ut inferis loquatur, et corona spinca coronetur (Apud August. eod. c. 12, lib. XVIII de Civ.). »
passages.english: 21. Through David himself: "I was turned," he says, "in distress, while the thorn was fixed [in me]" (Ps. 31:4). And the evangelists confirm this: that they placed a crown of thorns on his head, and he went out carrying his cross (Matt. 27:29; Mark 15:17; John 19:17). That ram also signified this, which, caught by its horns in thorns, was sacrificed in place of Isaac (Gen. 22:13). And the Sibyl declares: "That he may speak to those below, and be crowned with a crown of thorns" (in Augustine, the same chapter, City of God book 18).
passages.notes: "M'it" read as "exiit" (went out). "III" before "spinis" seems a stray mark. "Ut inferis loquatur" is uncertain; it may be a corruption.

passages.original: Cum ergo accepisset Jesus acetum plenum felle, ait : Consummatum est, et inclinato capite. tradidit spiritum (Joan. XIX, 28. etc.). Et per David hanc herbam non facuit dicens : Asperges me hyssopo, et mundabor (Pa. L, 9). Fatetur et Sibylla : < Ad cibum autem, ait, fel. et ad sitim acetum dederunt, P inhospitalitatis hanc monstrabunt mensam (Apud Augustin., ubi supra). t Ad hæc quoque Virgiliarum illud respondet (Eclog. 4. v. 44): Occidet et serpens, et fellax herba veneni.
passages.english: When, then, Jesus had received the vinegar full of gall, he said: "It is finished," and bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:28 etc.). And through David he did not pass over this herb in silence, saying: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed" (Ps. 50:9). And the Sibyl declares: "For food," she says, "they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar; they will display this table of inhospitality" (in Augustine, as above). To these things that [line] of Virgil also answers (Eclogue 4.24): "The serpent too will die, and the deceitful herb of poison."
passages.notes: "non facuit" read as "non tacuit" (did not pass over in silence). "Virgiliarum" read as "Virgilianum". The correct reference is Eclogue 4.24.

passages.original: Et hæc evangelistæ dicentes confirmant : Postquam crucifixus est Jesus, tenebræ fuctæ sunt per universam terram a sexta hora usque in nonam (Ma th. XXVII, 45). Et iterum : Postquam emisit spirtum Jesus, velumtempli scissum est in duas paries a sommo usque ad deorsum (Ibid., 51). Dicit et Paulus ap ostolus : i Cum conversi fuerint ad Christum, auferetur velamen (II Cor. III, 16). Fatetur et Sibylla : < Templi roro velum, ait, scindetur, et medio die nox erit lenebrosa nimbis in tribus horis. »
passages.english: And the evangelists confirm these things, saying: "After Jesus was crucified, there was darkness over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth" (Matt. 27:45). And again: "After Jesus gave up his spirit, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom" (ibid. 51). The apostle Paul also says: "When they have turned to Christ, the veil will be taken away" (2 Cor. 3:16). And the Sibyl declares: "The veil of the temple," she says, "will be torn, and at midday there will be a night dark with clouds for three hours."
passages.notes: "roro" is probably a corruption, perhaps of "vero" (and) or "toto" (whole), and is not rendered.

passages.original: Testatur et I aulus dicens Corinthiis : Tradidi enim vobis in primis quod et accepi, quia Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris secundum Scripturas, et quia sepultus est, et quia resurrexit tertia die secundum Scripturus (I Cor. XV, 3). Fatetur et Sibylla (Ubi supra) : « Et morte morietur, ait, tribus diebus, somno suscepto. »
passages.english: Paul too testifies, saying to the Corinthians: "For I handed on to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Cor. 15:3). And the Sibyl declares (as above): "And he will die by death," she says, "for three days, having taken on sleep."

passages.original: 29. Isaias propheta dicit: Exsurgent mortui, et v excitabuntur qui in monumentis sunt, et q exsultabunt omnes qui sunt in terra. Ros enim qui a te est, medicina illis est (Isai. XXVI., 19). Itæc firmat Matthæus evangelista, dicens : Terra mota est, et pe ræ scissæ sunt, et monumenta aperta sunt et multa corpora sanctorum dormientium surrexerunt. Et exeuntes de monumentis post resurrectionem ipsius, venerunt in sanctam civitatem et apparuerunt multis (Matth. XXVIX, 51, etc.). Dicit et Paulus: Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quæ sartum sunt quærite, ubi Christus est in dextera. Dei sedens (Coloss. III, 4). Testatur et Petrus aposto- Ius dicens : Ideo et mortuis evangelizatum de (1 Petr. IV, 6). Fatetur et Sibylla : Tartareumque chaos monstravit terra dehiscens. Inquirens tetri ponas r infringet Averni, Sauclorum sedenim cunctæ lux liber a carni
passages.english: 29. The prophet Isaiah says: "The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will be raised, and all who are on the earth will rejoice. For the dew that is from you is healing for them" (Isa. 26:19). The evangelist Matthew confirms these things, saying: "The earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many" (Matt. 27:51 etc.). Paul also says: "If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God" (Col. 3:1). The apostle Peter too testifies, saying: "For this reason the gospel was preached to the dead also" (1 Pet. 4:6). And the Sibyl declares: "The earth, gaping open, showed the chaos of Tartarus. Seeking [them], he will break the punishments of foul Avernus; for all the light of the saints, free to the flesh [...]"
passages.notes: Corrections: Hæc, petræ, sursum, Col. 3:1. The Sibylline verses are corrupt and the passage breaks off: "ponas" read as "poenas", "Sauclorum sedenim" as "Sanctorum etenim"; "lux liber a carni" is unclear and the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: Respondetur quod hi qui suscitati sunt, denuo mortui, cum sic dormientibus hodieque requiescunt : Christum autem Paulus apostolus dicit ideo primitias dormientium, quia surgens ex mortuis, jam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur (Rom. VI, 9). Fatetur et Sibylla : i Tunc ab inferis regressus, ad lucem veniet primus; resurrectionis principio revocatis ostenso. »
passages.english: The answer is that those who were raised died again, and rest even today along with those who are asleep. But the apostle Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep for this reason: because, rising from the dead, he no longer dies, and death will no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). And the Sibyl declares: "Then, having returned from those below, he will come first to the light, the beginning of the resurrection having been shown to those called back."
passages.notes: "cum sic dormientibus" probably for "cum ceteris dormientibus" (with the others who sleep).

passages.original: XX, 27). Testatur et Joannes in Epistola sua, dicens : Quod audivimus, quod vidimus nostris oculis, et manus nostræ contracteverunt de Verbo vitæ, el vita palam facta est nobis (I Joan. I, f). 6t Paulus dicit : Apparuit Cephæ, postea undecim. Deinde apparuit plus quam quingentis fratribus simul, ex quibus plures manent usque adhuc (I Cor. xv, & et seq ). Item : Si Christas prædicatur quia resurrexit a mortuis, quomodo dicunt quidam in vobis, quiu resurrectio mortuorum non est (Ibid., 12)? Dicit et Maro (Eclog. IV, v. 15. 14) : Te duce, si qua manent sceleris vestigia nostri, Irrila perpetua solvent formidine terras.
passages.english: [...] 20:27). John too testifies in his Epistle, saying: "What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled concerning the Word of life, and the life was made manifest to us" (1 John 1:1). And Paul says: "He appeared to Cephas, then to the eleven. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom most remain until now" (1 Cor. 15:5 ff.). Again: "If Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" (ibid. 12). And Maro also says (Eclogue 4.13–14): "Under your leadership, if any traces of our crime remain, made void, they will free the lands from perpetual fear."
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-reference (John 20:27). "Irrila" read as "Irrita". Paul's text has "the twelve"; this one reads "the eleven".

passages.original: 34. Jeremias propheta : Eece dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et consummabo super domum Israel, et super domum Juda Testamentum novum, s non secundum Testamentum quod dedi patribus eorum (Jer. xxxi, 31 ; Hebr. VIII, 8). t Et paulo post : Hoc est Testamentum quod dispono ad eo:, dans leges meas in mentibus eorum, et in cordibus corum u superascribam eas : et non aocebit unusquisque fratrem suum dicens : , Cognosce Dominum. Quia omnes cognoscent me a majore usque ad minorem eorum (Jer. XXXI, 33, 34). Et per Isaiam : Ecce ego nova facio, quæ nunc orientur (Isa. XL'II, 19). Et iterum : His vero qui mihi serviunt, nomen nominabitur novum (Isa. LXII, 2). Intelligitur utique Christianum, quod nomen terras obtinuit. Dicit ct David : Cantate Domino canticum novum; cantate Domino, omnis terra (Psal. XCV, 1). Quis h:rc nisi cæcus corde, impleta non videat? Firmat a hæc Dominus in Evangelio Matthæi. Omnis, ait, scriba eruditus in regno Dei, similis est tiro prof renti de b thesauris sus nova et vetera (Matth. xit, Et nerum : Quod nascitur c de Spiritu, spiritus est (Joan. III, 6). Testatur et Paulus : Primus, ait, homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo de cælo d cælestus. Quomodo portavimus imaginem terreni, induamus et imaginem eam qui de cælo est (I Cor. xv, 47, 49). Et iterum : Renovamini, ait, spiritu mentis ve- stræ, et induite novum hominem, b eum qui secundum Deum creatus est (Ephes. IV, 28). Item : Si qua, ait, in Christo nova creatura, vetera transierunt, et ecce facta sunt nova (II Cur. v, 17). Dicit et Maro (Ecloy. iv, v. 8, 9) : Quo ferrea primum Desinit, ac toto surgit gens aurea muodo.
passages.english: 34. The prophet Jeremiah: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I gave to their fathers" (Jer. 31:31; Heb. 8:8). And a little later: "This is the covenant which I appoint for them, putting my laws in their minds, and on their hearts I will write them; and each one will not teach his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord.' For all will know me, from the greatest to the least of them" (Jer. 31:33, 34). And through Isaiah: "Behold, I make new things, which will now spring forth" (Isa. 43:19). And again: "But to those who serve me a new name will be given" (Isa. 62:2). This is certainly understood [as] Christian, a name which has taken hold of the lands. David also says: "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth" (Ps. 95:1). Who but one blind of heart would not see these things fulfilled? The Lord confirms these things in the Gospel of Matthew. "Every scribe," he says, "learned in the kingdom of God is like a man bringing forth from his treasures new things and old" (Matt. 13:52). And again: "What is born of the Spirit is spirit" (John 3:6). Paul also testifies: "The first man," he says, "[was] from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also put on the image of him who is from heaven" (1 Cor. 15:47, 49). And again: "Be renewed," he says, "in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God" (Eph. 4:23–24). Likewise: "If anyone," he says, "[is] in Christ, [he is] a new creature; the old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be" (2 Cor. 5:17). Maro also says (Eclogue 4, lines 8–9): "In which the iron race first ceases, and a golden race arises in the whole world."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. Eece, tiro for viro, nerum for iterum, aocebit for docebit, muodo for mundo). 'consummabo ... Testamentum' follows the Vulgate of Hebrews. 'Ad eo:' read as 'ad eos'. 'Isa. XL'II, 19' read as 43:19. The Matthew reference is broken in the print ('xit,'). The Ephesians reference is printed as 4:28 (properly 4:23–24). 'Maro' is Virgil.

passages.original: 35. Per David prophetam dicunt: Propter te morte afficimur tota die, deputati sumus ut oves occisionis (Ps. XLIII, 22). Et iterum : Dedisti nos tamquam oves ad escam (Ibid., 12). Item ibi : Pretiosa in conspectu Domini mora sanctorum ejus (Ps. cxv, 6) Firmat hæc ipse in Evangelio, dicens : Ecce ego mitto vos sicut oves in medio luporum (Matth. x, 16). Et iterum : Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, in ri. tam æternam conservabit illam (Ibid., 29). Item : Trademini autem a fratribus, cognatis et amicis, et morte officient ex vobis; et eritis odio omnibus propter nomen meum. Qui autem sustinuerit usque in finem, hic salvus erit (Luc. xxi, 16). Et in Joanne : Nisi, ait, granum frumenti cadens in terram mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet; si autem mortuum fuerit, multum fructum affert (Joan. XII. 24). Testatur et Joannes apostolus, dicens : Sicut Christus pro nobis animam posuit, sic et nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere (I Joan. III, 16). Dicit et Paulus : Certus sum enim quia neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, e neque principatus, neque præsentia, neque futura (et concludit), neque creatura alia poterit nos separare a charitate Dei, quæce est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro (Rom. VIII, 38, 39). Ad haec illud Maronis (Eclog. IV, 15, 16) : h Permixtosque (ait) videbit Heroas divis, et ipse videbitur illis.
passages.english: 35. Through the prophet David they say: "For your sake we are put to death all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter" (Ps. 43:22). And again: "You have given us like sheep for food" (ibid., 12). Likewise there: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Ps. 115:6). He himself confirms these things in the Gospel, saying: "Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves" (Matt. 10:16). And again: "Whoever loses his life for my sake will keep it unto eternal life" (ibid., 39). Likewise: "You will be handed over by brothers, relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But whoever endures to the end, he will be saved" (Luke 21:16). And in John: "Unless," he says, "a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24). The apostle John also testifies, saying: "As Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for the brothers" (1 John 3:16). Paul also says: "For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come (and he concludes), nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom. 8:38, 39). To these [add] that [line] of Maro (Eclogue 4, 15–16): "And he will see heroes mingled with the gods (he says), and he himself will be seen by them."
passages.notes: 'mora' read as 'mors', 'officient' as 'afficient', 'in ri. tam' as 'in vitam'. The Matthew reference 'Ibid., 29' is as printed. 'Maro' is Virgil.

passages.original: 58. In David propheta : Adorabunt eum omnes reges terræ, omnes gentes servient illi (Ps. LXXI, 11). Et Isaias propheta : Gentes, ait, et reges qui tibi non ser- vierint, peribunt Isa. LX, 12). Et iterum : Ecce. ait Dominus, tollo in gentes manum meam, et in insulas tollam signum meum; et adducent filios tuos in gremio, filias autem tuas super humeros a tollent. Et erunt reges nutritores tui, et principes feminæ eorum psaltrices tuæ. Et super faciem terræ adorabunt te, et pulverem tuorum pedum lingent (Isa. XLIX. 22, etc.). Firmat hæc Dominus in Evangelio, dicens : HeMina Austri exsurget b in judicio cum generatione hac, et condemnabit cam. Venit enim a finibus terro' audire sapientiam Salomonis. Et ecce plus quam Salomon hic (Matth. XII, 42; Luc. XI. 31), Ideo plus hic, quia ad illum una. ad istum omnia regna venerunt. Sicut nunc nos, c qui lania credidimus et credimus, hæc impleri et cernimus et vidimus. Fatetur et Sibylla, dicens (Apud August. ubi supra) : Et corum hoc Domino reges sistentur ad unum.
passages.english: 58. In the prophet David: "All the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him" (Ps. 71:11). And the prophet Isaiah: "The nations," he says, "and kings that will not serve you will perish" (Isa. 60:12). And again: "Behold," says the Lord, "I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the islands I will raise my sign; and they will bring your sons in their bosom, and they will carry your daughters on their shoulders. And kings will be your foster-fathers, and their princesses your singers. And they will worship you face to the earth, and lick the dust of your feet" (Isa. 49:22 etc.). The Lord confirms these things in the Gospel, saying: "The queen of the South will rise up in the judgement with this generation and will condemn it. For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And behold, more than Solomon [is] here" (Matt. 12:42; Luke 11:31). [It is] 'more' here for this reason: because to him one kingdom came, to this one all kingdoms came. As now we, who have long believed and do believe, both discern and have seen these things fulfilled. The Sibyl also declares, saying (in Augustine, as above): "And before this Lord the kings will be set, all together."
passages.notes: The section number '58' is probably a misprint for 38. 'HeMina' read as 'Regina'. 'psaltrices' (singers) stands where the Vulgate has 'nutrices' (nurses). 'lania' read as 'jamdudum' (long since), which is uncertain. 'corum' read as 'coram' (before).

passages.original: 39. David propheta dicit: Nunc reges intelligite, a erudimini omnes qui judicatis terram. Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore. Continete a disciplinam, ne quando irascatur Dominus, et pereatis de via justa (Psal. II, 10, etc.). Et iterum : In conveniendo populos in unum, f et reges ut serviant Domino (Ps. CI, 23), # Dicit et Salomon : Diligite justitiam, qui judicatis terram (Sup. I, 1). Firmat hæc Dominus iu Evangelio, dicens : Tollite jugum meum super vos, et discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Matth. XI, 29). Et iterum : In qua mensura mensi fueritis, in ea remittetur vobis (Matth. VII. 2). Testatur in hæc Jacobus apostolus : Judicium, h inquit, sine misericordia illi qui non fecerit misericordiam. Superexaltat enim misericordia judicio (Jacob. II, 15). Paulus etiam orandum pro regibus i censet, et pro his qui in sublimitatibus sunt, ut quietam et tranquillam vitam agamus (I Tim. II, 2). Ad hæc Maro ait (Æneid. VI, v. 620) : Discite justitiam moniti, et non temnere divos.
passages.english: 39. The prophet David says: "Now, kings, understand; be instructed, all you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Hold fast to discipline, lest at some time the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way" (Ps. 2:10 etc.). And again: "When the peoples gather together, and kings, to serve the Lord" (Ps. 101:23). Solomon also says: "Love justice, you who judge the earth" (Wis. 1:1). The Lord confirms these things in the Gospel, saying: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart" (Matt. 11:29). And again: "With the measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you" (Matt. 7:2). The apostle James testifies to these things: "Judgement," he says, "without mercy to him who has not shown mercy. For mercy exalts itself over judgement" (James 2:13). Paul also judges that one should pray for kings and for those who are in high places, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life (1 Tim. 2:2). To these Maro says (Aeneid 6, line 620): "Be warned: learn justice, and not to scorn the gods."
passages.notes: 'Continete a disciplinam' read as 'Apprehendite disciplinam'. The reference 'Sup. I, 1' is to Wisdom (Sapientia) 1:1. The James reference is printed as 2:15.

passages.original: I At Spiritus Dei ante prædixit : spiritus etiam dæmonum confitendo tacere nequiverunt, et maxime qui ipsi dixerant Domino : Quid venisti ante tempus h perdere nos (Marc. 1, 24)? Hic tanta deorum illa turba fertorum atque incertorum quos Varro prodit; illi elim proceres et electi dii cum ipso rege suo Jove fulmina vibrante, consilio potentiaque (ut eorum cultores ferunt) metuendi , armisque terribiles, hie hie aliquid, si non pro mundo, saltem pro se 1 oportebat agere, ne scilicet unus eos perderet Crucifixus. Periisse vero et nos novimus, et David propheta eonfirmat dicens : Periit memoria eorum eum strepilu, et Domnus in æternum manet (Psal. IX, 8).
passages.english: But the Spirit of God foretold [this] beforehand; the spirits of demons too, by confessing, could not keep silent, and especially those who had themselves said to the Lord: "Why have you come before the time to destroy us?" (Mark 1:24). Here that great crowd of gods, certain and uncertain, which Varro sets out; those once-chief and select gods, with their king Jupiter himself brandishing thunderbolts, to be feared for their counsel and power (as their worshippers claim), and terrible in arms: here, here they ought to have done something, if not for the world, at least for themselves, namely so that one Crucified man should not destroy them. But that they have perished we too know, and the prophet David confirms it, saying: "Their memory has perished with a noise, and the Lord remains for ever" (Psalm 9:8).
passages.notes: The initial "I" and the letters "h" and "1" are taken as stray marks from the printed page. "fertorum" read as "certorum" (Varro's di certi and di incerti, the 'certain' and 'uncertain' gods); "elim" read as "olim". The repeated "hie hie" is read as "hic, hic" ('here, here'). The Mark citation is a loose recollection; the wording is closer to Matthew 8:29 ("ante tempus").

passages.original: Huic etiam capitulo, quæ supra posuimus verba un Sibyllæ conventum dicentis (Apud Augustin. ubi supra): n Dejiciet colles, valles extollet ab imo. Non erit iu rebus hominum sublime, vel altum. Cui consonana Maro dicit (Ecloga iv, v. 22) : Nec magno mentuent armenta leones.
passages.english: To this chapter also [belong] the words we set down above of the Sibyl, who agrees, saying (in Augustine, as above): "He will cast down the hills, he will raise the valleys from the depths. There will be nothing lofty or high in human affairs." In harmony with this Maro says (Eclogue 4, line 22): "Nor will the herds fear great lions."
passages.notes: 'un ... conventum' is corrupt and probably read 'Sibyllae convenientia' or similar; the opening sentence lacks a verb, so the sense is approximate. 'mentuent' read as 'metuent'.

passages.original: Ut illi quadringenti nonginta anni, et isti qui excurrunt ab adventu Salvatoris uque in m solutionem ejusdem diaboli, n concludant mille ann' s , in quibus ligatus est diabolus, ne ultra seduceret nationes, quas antea possederat in idololatriis. Quania autem virtute, ut ait beatæ memoriæ Augustinus (De Civit. Dei l. ix. c. 7, n. 2), pollebunt tunc sancti qui luctaturi sunt cum diabolo soluto, cum quo ligato tamis periculis dimicatur ? Jam enim, ut Paulus dicit, mysterium iniquitatis op eratur (II Thess.
passages.english: So that those four hundred and ninety years, and these which run from the coming of the Saviour up to the loosing of that same devil, may make up the thousand years in which the devil has been bound, so that he might no longer lead astray the nations which he had previously possessed in idolatries. But with how great strength, as Augustine of blessed memory says (City of God, book 20, ch. 8, no. 2), will the saints be powerful then, who are to wrestle with the devil when he is loosed, when even with him bound the struggle is waged amid such great dangers? For already, as Paul says, the mystery of iniquity is at work (2 Thess.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-argument; 'quadringenti nonginta' read as 'quadringenti nonaginta' (490), which is somewhat uncertain. 'tamis' read as 'tantis'. The Augustine reference is printed as 'l. ix. c. 7'. The text breaks off mid-reference.

passages.original: et omnis mons et insulæ 1 de locis suis motæ sunt, et reges terræ maximique tribuni, et divites, et nobiles, et servi absconde- runt se in speluncis et petris montium, dicentes montibus et petris : Cadite super nos, et abscondite nos a conspectu Patris sedentis super thronum, et ab ira Agni, quoniam venit dies magnus iræ illorum. Et quis poterit stare (Apoc. VI, 12, etc.) ? Dicit et Paulus apostolus : Ipse Dominus in jusu, in voce archangeli et in tuba Dei descendet de cœlo ( I Thess. IV, 5). Fatetur et Sibylla inter cætera dicens ( Apud August. lib. XVIII de Civit.c. 22) : Eripitur solis jubar, et chorus interit astris : Volvetur cœlum : m lunaris splendor obibit. Sed tuba tum sonitum tristem n demittet ab alto Orbe, gemens facinus miserum variosque labores. Tartareumque clinos monstrabit terra dehiscens.
passages.english: and every mountain and island was moved from its place, and the kings of the earth and the greatest tribunes, and the rich, and the nobles, and slaves hid themselves in caves and in the rocks of the mountains, saying to the mountains and rocks: "Fall on us, and hide us from the face of the Father seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come. And who will be able to stand?" (Rev. 6:12 etc.). The apostle Paul also says: "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God" (1 Thess. 4:15). The Sibyl also declares, among other things, saying (in Augustine, City of God book 18, ch. 23): "The radiance of the sun is snatched away, and the chorus of the stars perishes. The sky will be rolled up; the splendour of the moon will pass away. But then the trumpet will send down a sorrowful sound from the heights of the world, lamenting wretched crime and manifold toils. And the earth, gaping open, will show the abysses of Tartarus."
passages.notes: 'clinos' read as 'chaos' (abyss). 'jusu' read as 'jussu'. The Augustine chapter is printed as 22 (it is 23).

passages.original: Et iierum : Transivimus per ignem et aquam, et induxisti nos in refrigerium (Ibid., 12). Et Malachias proph ta : Ipse 1 introiit, ait, sicut ignis conflatorii, et sedebit conflans, et purgans sicut argentum et aurum, mel purgavit filios Levi ( Malach. III, 2 et seq.). Et in Evangelio Matthæus hæc de Domino confirmat dicens : ilic est qui baptizat in Spiritu sancto et igni, ferens ventitabrum in manu sua, et purgabit aream suam. Frumenta recondet n in horreo, paleas comburet igni inexstinguibili (Matth. III, 11 et 12). Et iterum ipse Dominus dicit: Prius quam cœlum et terra transeal, iota unum, aut unus apex non cadet ex lege, o qui non impleatur (Matth. v, 18). Et Petrus Apostolus : Qui autem nunc sunt cœli, eodem verbo repositi sunt, igni reservandi in diem judicii (II Petr. III, 7). Et paulo post: Properantes, ait, ad præsentiam Domini, per quam cæli ardentes solventur, et elementa ignis ardore decoquentur (Ibid., 12). Dicil et Paulus : Quia et ipsa creatura liberabitur a servitute P corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei (Rom. VIII, 21). Fatetur et Sibylla dicens (Ubi supra) : Omnia cessabunt, tellus confracta peribit. Sic pariter fontes torrentur, fluminaque igni.
passages.english: And again: "We passed through fire and water, and you led us into refreshment" (ibid., 12). And the prophet Malachi: "He himself," he says, "will come in like a refiner's fire, and he will sit refining and purifying as silver and gold, and he will purify the sons of Levi" (Mal. 3:2 ff.). And in the Gospel Matthew confirms these things about the Lord, saying: "This is he who baptises in the Holy Spirit and fire, carrying a winnowing fan in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor. He will store the wheat in the barn; he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire" (Matt. 3:11–12). And again the Lord himself says: "Before heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will fall from the law that is not fulfilled" (Matt. 5:18). And the apostle Peter: "But the heavens which now are have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgement" (2 Pet. 3:7). And a little later: "Hastening," he says, "to the presence of the Lord, through which the heavens will be dissolved in burning, and the elements will be melted by the heat of fire" (ibid., 12). Paul also says: "For creation itself also will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God" (Rom. 8:21). The Sibyl also declares, saying (as above): "All things will cease; the earth, shattered, will perish. Likewise springs and rivers are scorched with fire."
passages.notes: 'introiit' is rendered as future, as the sense requires. 'mel purgavit' read as 'et purgabit'. 'ventitabrum' read as 'ventilabrum'.
